pos: part. adj. / v. (in the act of ceasing to live)
etymology: From die, Anglo-Saxon deagan, kindred with the Norse deyja — to lose life, to expire.
biblical_def:
Now there were seven brethren: and the first took a wife, and dying left no seed. As dying, and, behold, we live. By faith Jacob, when he was a dying, blessed both the sons of Joseph. Shall we be consumed with dying?

Scripture never treats dying as a private biological event to be managed and hidden. It is the last public act of a life, and Jacob's dying was the occasion of his greatest faith — leaning on his staff to bless his grandsons, not sedated past speech. Paul lists dying beside living as one more circumstance the gospel has already answered: as dying, and, behold, we live. The believer's dying is swallowed up, not by denial, but by resurrection. The Israelites who cried out at Numb 17:13 feared dying as final exposure to holiness unmediated by a priest; the believer under the Mediator has no such terror left, only the last obedience of faith.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from DIE: to be deprived of life; to cease to live; to expire; used of the last act or process of losing animal life.
webster_full: DIE, v.i. To be deprived of life; to cease to live; to expire.
To lose vital action in the whole body, as opposed to a lingering, partial death.
To languish, sink, or perish, as by inches; to become gradually weaker.
In Scripture, used also of spiritual death, the separation of the soul from the favor of God.
DYING, ppr. Losing life; expiring; drawing toward the close of natural life.
scriptures: Now there were seven brethren: and the first took a wife, and dying left no seed.
As unknown, and yet well known; as dying, and, behold, we live; as chastened, and not killed;
By faith Jacob, when he was a dying, blessed both the sons of Joseph; and worshipped, leaning upon the top of his staff.
Whosoever cometh any thing near unto the tabernacle of the LORD shall die: shall we be consumed with dying?
corruption_summary: The age has professionalized dying into a private, sanitized procedure — a passing, spoken of in whispers and euphemism, managed out of sight so the living need never watch it or name it.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern speech prefers "passed," "lost," or "transitioned" to the plain word dying, not from tenderness but from a deeper discomfort: a culture with no doctrine of the resurrection cannot bear to look at death honestly, so it dresses the word up until it disappears.

Scripture does the opposite. It names dying and then answers it — as dying, and, behold, we live is not euphemism but confrontation followed by triumph. A generation taught to flinch from the word will be unprepared for the hour it names.
roots_summary: The root is simply DIE (Heb. muth, Gk. apothnesko), the plainest word in the biblical vocabulary for the wages of sin, here in its present participle.
roots_lines: Dying is the ongoing form of dying — a process Scripture is willing to watch and narrate.
Jacob's dying blessing shows faith active at the very edge of life.
Paul's as dying, and, behold, we live sets dying inside resurrection logic, not apart from it.
Numbers 17:13 shows dying feared as exposure to holiness without a mediator.
The New Testament never asks the believer to deny dying, only to see past it.
usage: As dying, and, behold, we live — the apostolic refusal to let dying have the last word.
When he was a dying, blessed both the sons of Joseph — faith does its clearest work at the deathbed.
Shall we be consumed with dying? — the cry of a people who had not yet been given a Mediator.

pos: v. (past tense of befall; happened unto, came to pass for)
etymology: Anglo-Saxon befeallan, be- + feallan, to fall — literally, to fall upon or come down upon a person.
biblical_def:
And they came unto Jacob their father unto the land of Canaan, and told him all that befell unto them. That will be worse unto thee than all the evil that befell thee from thy youth until now. Serving the Lord with all humility of mind, and with many tears, and temptations, which befell me. And they that saw it told them how it befell to him that was possessed with the devil.

Befell is Scripture's ordinary word for providence recounted after the fact — Jacob's sons report what befell them in Egypt, and Paul catalogues the temptations that befell him in ministry. The word carries no doctrine of chance; a thing that befalls a man in the biblical narrative is a thing that fell upon him from a hand higher than circumstance. To ask what befell someone is to ask for the plain report, trusting that the report itself will be read under God's government of events.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from BEFALL: to happen to; to occur to, as a fortune, event or accident; used chiefly of that which happens by chance or the course of things.
webster_full: BEFALL, v.t. To happen to; to occur to, as a fortune, event or accident.
There shall no evil befall thee. Psalms.
BEFALL, v.i. To happen; to come to pass.
BEFELL, pret. of Befall.
Used in narrative to introduce the report of what has occurred to a person or company.
scriptures: And they came unto Jacob their father unto the land of Canaan, and told him all that befell unto them; saying,
For I swear by the LORD, if thou go not forth, there will not tarry one with thee this night: and that will be worse unto thee than all the evil that befell thee from thy youth until now.
Serving the Lord with all humility of mind, and with many tears, and temptations, which befell me by the lying in wait of the Jews:
Mar 5:16
And they that saw it told them how it befell to him that was possessed with the devil, and also concerning the swine.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Befell is a plain narrative verb, and the age has not found reason to weaponize it.

The principle worth recovering is the one the word quietly assumes: a thing that befalls a man is not random. Joab's warning to David and Paul's list of what befell him in Acts both take for granted that a report of events is also a report of providence.
roots_summary: No biblical Hebrew or Greek headword; the field is providence (Heb. qarah, to meet or befall) narrated in the plain past tense.
roots_lines: Befell is the past tense of befall — a fall from above onto a life.
Genesis uses it for the sons' report of Egypt to their father.
2 Samuel uses it for a whole life's accumulated evil.
Acts uses it for the trials of an apostle's ministry.
Mark uses it for the report of a single deliverance.
usage: Told him all that befell unto them — the plain report that assumes God's hand in the events reported.
Worse unto thee than all the evil that befell thee — a lifetime's providence summarized in one clause.
Temptations which befell me — Paul's own ministry read as a series of things that fell upon him, not merely things he chose.

etymology: Anglo-Saxon wisra, comparative of wis, wise — of superior discernment, judgment, or skill.
biblical_def:
For the children of this world are in their generation wiser than the children of light. The sluggard is wiser in his own conceit than seven men that can render a reason. Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men. Thou through thy commandments hast made me wiser than mine enemies.

Scripture's use of wiser is almost always comparative in the most searching sense: wiser measured against what standard, and whose. The Lord's own parable concedes that the children of this world are wiser than the children of light in their generation — worldly cunning genuinely outperforms careless piety at worldly business. But Paul's wiser than men belongs to God alone, and it exposes every human claim to superior wisdom as, at best, borrowed. The sluggard wiser in his own conceit is the counterfeit: a man crowned wise by nobody but himself. True wiser comes only from the commandments, as the psalmist found — not from outpacing one's age, but from outlasting one's own opinion of it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from WISE: having the power of discerning and judging correctly, or of discriminating between truth and falsehood, right and wrong; comparative degree.
webster_full: WISE, a. Having the power of discerning and judging correctly, or of discriminating between truth and falsehood, right and wrong.
Possessing sound judgment and prudence in the choice of means to accomplish a good end.
Wise is applicable to the choice of good ends as well as good means, and this is its most important sense.
WISER, a. Comparative of Wise; more wise; excelling another in discernment or judgment.
The truly wise man regards the will of God as the supreme rule of judgment.
scriptures: Luk 16:8
And the lord commended the unjust steward, because he had done wisely: for the children of this world are in their generation wiser than the children of light.
The sluggard is wiser in his own conceit than seven men that can render a reason.
Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men; and the weakness of God is stronger than men.
Thou through thy commandments hast made me wiser than mine enemies: for they are ever with me.
corruption_summary: Chronological snobbery has made wiser a settled fact of the calendar: the present age is assumed wiser than every prior one simply for having come later, and Scripture is read as the record of a less-informed past.
corruption_paragraphs: Every progressive claim to moral advance leans on an unexamined wiser — we, being modern, are wiser than the apostles, the reformers, the text itself. It is Proverbs 26:16 restaged at civilizational scale: a sluggard's conceit, now shared by a whole culture, mistaking the passage of time for the accumulation of wisdom.
1 Corinthians 1:25 stands against this permanently. The foolishness of God is wiser than men settles which wiser outranks which, in every century, without appeal.
roots_summary: From chakam (Heb.) and sophos (Gk.), wisdom as skill in living rightly before God — here in the comparative degree that Scripture is careful to qualify.
roots_lines: Wiser is always a comparison, and Scripture insists on naming the terms of the comparison.
Luke 16:8 grants worldly wiser its narrow, worldly domain.
1 Corinthians 1:25 revokes every human claim to wiser before the foolishness of God.
Psalm 119:98 locates true wiser in the commandments, not in cleverness.
Proverbs 26:16 exposes self-conferred wiser as the sluggard's private delusion.
usage: Children of this world... wiser than the children of light — a narrow commendation, not a compliment to worldliness.
The foolishness of God is wiser than men — the verse that ends every argument from progress.
Made me wiser than mine enemies — wisdom traced to the commandments, not to the age.

pos: adj. / v. (moderately cold; to allay heat, passion, or ardor)
etymology: Anglo-Saxon col, kindred with cald, cold — a moderate degree of cold, neither warm nor freezing.
biblical_def:
And they heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden in the cool of the day: and Adam and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God amongst the trees of the garden. Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water, and cool my tongue; for I am tormented in this flame.

Scripture's two great uses of cool sit at opposite ends of a life. In Eden it is the ordinary mercy of an evening breeze, the very hour God chose to walk with man before sin drove him behind the trees — the cool of the day was fellowship's appointed time, now remembered as the hour it was lost. In torment it is the mercy denied: the rich man begs for one drop to cool his tongue and is refused, because the years he might have sought coolness of soul he spent seeking only comfort of body. The same word marks the garden he forfeited and the drop he cannot obtain.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): moderately cold; between hot and cold, in such a degree as to give a pleasant sensation, without a chilling effect; also, to allay heat, passion, or excitement.
webster_full: COOL, a. Moderately cold; between hot and cold; as, cool air; a cool day.
Not ardent, warm, or zealous; wanting warmth or affection.
Manifesting coldness or dislike; not cordial.
COOL, v.t. To allay or moderate heat; to abate the ardor of passion; to calm or moderate excitement.
COOL, n. A moderate state of cold; a temperate state of the air between hot and cold.
scriptures: Gen 3:8
And they heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden in the cool of the day: and Adam and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God amongst the trees of the garden.
And he cried and said, Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water, and cool my tongue; for I am tormented in this flame.
corruption_summary: The word has been promoted from a temperature to the supreme cultural virtue: whatever is cool needs no further justification, and whatever is not cool needs no further condemnation.
corruption_paragraphs: A generation that measures worth by cool has replaced the fear of the Lord with the fear of embarrassment. Ministries reshape worship, dress, and speech chasing the approval of a standard that changes by the season and answers to no one.

Genesis 3:8 already shows what is lost when man prefers hiding to walking with God in the cool of the day. The rich man in Luke 16 spent his cool comfort on himself and had none left to beg for. Cool bought at the price of holiness is bought at the highest price there is.
roots_summary: No single Hebrew or Greek headword; the field is temperance and the fear of God set against the pursuit of comfort and approval.
roots_lines: Cool of the day names the hour, not merely the temperature.
Eden's cool was the setting for fellowship, now the setting for hiding.
Luke 16 makes cool the smallest mercy, denied to a man who sought comfort over God.
Neither passage treats cool as a virtue in itself — only as a gift or a memory.
Modern usage inverts this, making cool the standard other virtues must answer to.
usage: The cool of the day — the hour of fellowship man forfeited by sin.
Cool my tongue — the smallest possible request, and still refused.
Neither Eden's cool nor Lazarus's drop was ever man's to command.

etymology: Anglo-Saxon bitan, to bite — the wound inflicted by teeth or, in Scripture, by the serpent.
biblical_def:
And the LORD said unto Moses, Make thee a fiery serpent, and set it upon a pole: and it shall come to pass, that every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live. And Moses made a serpent of brass, and put it upon a pole, and it came to pass, that if a serpent had bitten any man, when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived.

Bitten belongs to one of the clearest types in the Old Testament. Israel, having spoken against God and against Moses, was bitten by fiery serpents sent as judgment; the cure God appointed was not medicine but a look — whoever was bitten and looked at the brass serpent lived. The Lord himself claims this narrow, strange episode as the pattern of his own lifting up: as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up. The man bitten by sin has no remedy in himself; he is healed only by looking, in simple faith, at the thing lifted up for him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from BITE: to seize with the teeth, so as to enter, pierce, or wound; the past participle denoting the wound already inflicted.
webster_full: BITE, v.t. To seize with the teeth, so as to enter, pierce, or wound.
To pain, distress or afflict; used figuratively.
BITTEN, pp. Seized, pierced, or wounded with the teeth; figuratively, stung or afflicted.
Applied in Scripture to the wound of the fiery serpents in the wilderness.
Also used, in later English, of frost, cold, or remorse, which bite or wound as a serpent.
scriptures: Num 21:8
And the LORD said unto Moses, Make thee a fiery serpent, and set it upon a pole: and it shall come to pass, that every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live.
Num 21:9
And Moses made a serpent of brass, and put it upon a pole, and it came to pass, that if a serpent had bitten any man, when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Bitten survives as a plain narrative word tied to one of the Old Testament's most deliberately typological events.

The principle to recover is the one Christ himself named: the man already bitten cannot cure himself by effort, only by looking. Every substitute gospel that asks the bitten sinner to strive rather than look has missed the pattern God set in the wilderness on purpose.
roots_summary: From nashak (Heb.), to bite, used of the serpent's judgment in Numbers 21, fulfilled in the type Christ names in John 3:14.
roots_lines: Bitten names the wound, not the cure.
The cure God appointed was a look, not an antidote.
Numbers 21 sets the pattern Christ claims for himself in John 3:14-15.
The bitten man who looked lived; the bitten man who trusted his own remedy did not.
The serpent that bit is answered by the serpent lifted up — judgment answered by judgment borne.
usage: Every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live — the whole gospel compressed into a wilderness sentence.
If a serpent had bitten any man — no exception is made; the bite is universal among the complaining camp.
Christ's own citation of this event makes bitten the type of every sinner under judgment.

etymology: Anglo-Saxon wacra, comparative of wac, weak, pliant — lacking strength or firmness.
biblical_def:
Likewise, ye husbands, dwell with them according to knowledge, giving honour unto the wife, as unto the weaker vessel, and as being heirs together of the grace of life; that your prayers be not hindered. Now there was long war between the house of Saul and the house of David: but David waxed stronger and stronger, and the house of Saul waxed weaker and weaker.

Peter's weaker vessel is not an insult but an instruction: because the wife is the weaker vessel, the husband is commanded to dwell with her according to knowledge and to give her honour, on pain of hindered prayers. The word describes a physical and social reality, not a spiritual or moral one — nothing in Scripture makes the woman weaker in faith, virtue, or standing as an heir together of the grace of life. The command rests entirely on the husband: greater strength obligates greater honour, never greater license. 2 Samuel's weaker and weaker is a different sense entirely, the plain waning of a rival house before God's chosen king, useful chiefly by contrast — Saul's house weakens under judgment, while Peter's weaker vessel is strengthened by honour, not diminished by it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from WEAK: wanting physical strength; feeble; not able to sustain a great weight, force, or opposition; comparative degree.
webster_full: WEAK, a. Wanting physical strength; feeble; infirm.
Not able to sustain a great weight, force, or opposition.
Not vigorous in mind; wanting force of intellect, judgment or resolution.
WEAKER, a. Comparative of Weak; less strong or vigorous.
In 1 Peter, applied to the wife as the weaker vessel, requiring the husband's honour and knowledge, not his contempt.
scriptures: Likewise, ye husbands, dwell with them according to knowledge, giving honour unto the wife, as unto the weaker vessel, and as being heirs together of the grace of life; that your prayers be not hindered.
Now there was long war between the house of Saul and the house of David: but David waxed stronger and stronger, and the house of Saul waxed weaker and weaker.
corruption_summary: Egalitarian readings strip the weaker vessel of its plain meaning entirely, treating Peter's honest description of physical difference as an embarrassment to be explained away rather than a command to be obeyed.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern instinct is to protest that weaker cannot really mean weaker, and so to soften Peter's word until the command built upon it — giving honour, dwelling according to knowledge — loses its foundation. The complementarian reading needs no apology: the text assigns strength a duty, not a rank.

A husband who uses his strength to belittle rather than to honour has inverted 1 Peter 3:7 completely, and Peter warns him plainly that his prayers, not his wife's submission, are what will be hindered.
roots_summary: From asthenes (Gk.), without strength, used by Peter of the wife's vessel in a household economy of honour, not of worth.
roots_lines: Weaker vessel describes strength, not standing before God.
The command in 1 Peter 3:7 falls on the stronger party, not the weaker.
Heirs together of the grace of life rules out any reading that makes weaker mean lesser.
2 Samuel 3:1 uses weaker of a house under judgment, a different sense entirely.
Dishonour of the weaker vessel is named as a direct hindrance to a husband's own prayers.
usage: As unto the weaker vessel — a description that obligates honour, not one that excuses contempt.
Heirs together of the grace of life — the weaker vessel is a full co-heir, never a lesser one.
Waxed weaker and weaker — the plain decline of a house under God's judgment, not a household analogy.

etymology: Anglo-Saxon hefigra, comparative of hefig, heavy — weighty, burdensome, pressing down.
biblical_def:
Even to day is my complaint bitter: my stroke is heavier than my groaning. A stone is heavy, and the sand weighty; but a fool's wrath is heavier than them both.

Job's heavier measures affliction against his own capacity to voice it — the stroke he bears outweighs even his groaning, which was already his greatest exertion of grief. Proverbs sets heavier against the two standard images of physical weight in the ancient world, stone and sand, and finds a fool's wrath heavier still, because it presses down on everyone near it with no natural limit, unlike a stone that can at least be measured and set down. Both uses agree that heavier is not decoration but arithmetic: Scripture weighs grief and sin as real quantities, bearing down on real people, never lighter than they feel.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from HEAVY: having great weight; ponderous; hard to be borne, as sorrow, affliction, or a burden of guilt; comparative degree.
webster_full: HEAVY, a. Having great weight; ponderous.
Sorrowful, grievous, afflictive; oppressive to the mind.
Wanting cheerfulness or animation; dull, sluggish, torpid.
HEAVIER, a. Comparative of Heavy; of greater weight, or more oppressive.
Applied figuratively to guilt, wrath, or grief that presses upon the soul as a weight presses upon the body.
scriptures: Job 23:2
Even to day is my complaint bitter: my stroke is heavier than my groaning.
Pro 27:3
A stone is heavy, and the sand weighty; but a fool's wrath is heavier than them both.
corruption_summary: A therapeutic culture that has abolished shame has no scale left for heavier; sin is relabeled a mistake, a condition, or a journey, and nothing is allowed to weigh what Scripture says it weighs.
corruption_paragraphs: Job did not manage his affliction with language designed to make it lighter than it was; he called his stroke heavier than his groaning and let the weight stand. A generation trained to minimize its own guilt has lost the vocabulary to say a thing is heavier without apologizing for saying so.

Proverbs 27:3 is a warning worth recovering precisely because it will not be softened: a fool's wrath outweighs stone and sand, and the modern instinct to treat anger as merely an emotion to be processed ignores how much it actually presses down on everyone underneath it.
roots_summary: From kabed (Heb.), heavy, glorious, weighty — the same root that gives glory its sense of weightiness, here turned toward affliction and wrath.
roots_lines: Heavier is Scripture's arithmetic of affliction, not its poetry.
Job's stroke outweighs even his loudest grief.
Proverbs sets a fool's wrath against literal stone and sand and finds it heavier than both.
Neither passage offers a technique for making the weight lighter, only for bearing it rightly.
The same root that makes glory weighty makes affliction and wrath heavy — Scripture does not treat any of them as trivial.
usage: My stroke is heavier than my groaning — grief that outweighs even its own expression.
A fool's wrath is heavier than them both — anger weighed against stone and sand, and found the worse burden.
Neither verse asks the sufferer to pretend the weight is less than it is.

pos: n. pl. (from deal, v.; those who deal, especially treacherously)
etymology: Anglo-Saxon dael, a part or share — one who deals gives out a part; a treacherous dealer withholds what he owes.
biblical_def:
From the uttermost part of the earth have we heard songs, even glory to the righteous. But I said, My leanness, my leanness, woe unto me! the treacherous dealers have dealt treacherously; yea, the treacherous dealers have dealt very treacherously. For the house of Israel and the house of Judah have dealt very treacherously against me, saith the LORD. Why do we deal treacherously every man against his brother, by profaning the covenant of our fathers?

Isaiah's dealers is doubled for emphasis: the treacherous dealers have dealt treacherously, a construction the Authorized Version uses nowhere lightly. This is not ordinary commerce but covenant betrayal named as business — men who deal falsely with one another the way a nation deals falsely with God, treating trust itself as the commodity to be spent. Jeremiah applies the same charge to Israel and Judah directly against the LORD, and Malachi turns it inward, against brother and brother, tied explicitly to profaning the covenant of the fathers. Dealers, in Scripture, is never a neutral trade name; it is what a covenant people become the moment they treat their word as negotiable.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from DEAL: one who deals or trades; in the plural, those engaged in traffic or exchange, whether honestly or, as often in Scripture, treacherously.
webster_full: DEAL, v.t. To divide; to distribute in parts.
DEAL, v.i. To transact business; to traffic; to trade.
To behave or act in any manner toward others, well or ill.
DEALER, n. One who deals; a trader, or one who transacts business with another.
DEALERS, n. pl. Traders; in Scripture usage, often those who deal falsely or treacherously with others.
scriptures: From the uttermost part of the earth have we heard songs, even glory to the righteous. But I said, My leanness, my leanness, woe unto me! the treacherous dealers have dealt treacherously; yea, the treacherous dealers have dealt very treacherously.
Jer 5:11
For the house of Israel and the house of Judah have dealt very treacherously against me, saith the LORD.
Mal 2:10
Have we not all one father? hath not one God created us? why do we deal treacherously every man against his brother, by profaning the covenant of our fathers?
corruption_summary: Commerce has softened dealer into a neutral, even respectable title — a car dealer, an art dealer, a dealer in antiques — while the biblical dealers is always the treacherous kind, and the softening quietly retires the word's original warning.
corruption_paragraphs: The KJV's dealers is never a compliment. It names men who spend other people's trust as currency, and Isaiah's doubled treacherous dealers have dealt treacherously reads almost as a legal indictment, repeated for the record.

Malachi ties the same charge to covenant-breaking between brothers, which is the deeper corruption still current: a culture that treats promises, vows, and contracts as merely negotiable has not modernized dealing, it has simply stopped naming it treachery.
roots_summary: From bagad (Heb.), to deal treacherously or act covertly, the very root behind Isaiah's doubled construction.
roots_lines: Dealers in the Authorized Version is almost always modified by treacherously.
Isaiah doubles the charge for emphasis: dealt treacherously, twice, of the same men.
Jeremiah applies dealers directly to covenant unfaithfulness toward the LORD.
Malachi applies the same charge horizontally, brother against brother.
None of the three passages treats dealing falsely as ordinary business practice.
usage: The treacherous dealers have dealt treacherously — Scripture's own emphatic doubling of the charge.
Dealt very treacherously against me — covenant-breaking named as business against God himself.
Deal treacherously every man against his brother — the same treachery, turned horizontal.

pos: n. (one who drives, urges, or compels; a taskmaster)
etymology: Anglo-Saxon drifan, to drive, urge forward — one who compels men or beasts to labor or motion.
biblical_def:
He scorneth the multitude of the city, neither regardeth he the crying of the driver. And Pharaoh commanded the same day the taskmasters of the people, and their officers, saying. And the taskmasters of the people went out, and their officers, and they spake to the people, saying, Thus saith Pharaoh, I will not give you straw.

Driver in Job describes the wild ass, indifferent to the very sound that terrifies a beast of burden — the crying of the driver, which controls every ordinary animal, has no power over a creature God has set free by nature. Exodus supplies the human counterpart in full: Pharaoh's taskmasters and officers are drivers of the harshest kind, doubling labor and withholding straw in the same breath, the record's plainest picture of bondage administered by men over men. Between the two stands the whole argument of the exodus: a driver's power reaches only as far as the LORD allows it, and the God who let Pharaoh's drivers oppress Israel for a season is the same God who broke every driver's authority at the Red Sea.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from DRIVE: one who drives; one who urges forward, compels, or governs by force, as a taskmaster over laborers or a driver of cattle.
webster_full: DRIVE, v.t. To impel or urge forward by force; to compel to move.
To urge, hurry, or press; to compel to act, speak, or proceed.
DRIVER, n. One who drives; one who urges or compels others to labor or motion.
In Scripture, applied to the taskmasters set over the Israelites in Egyptian bondage.
Also, one who drives cattle, or, figuratively, one who is himself driven by ambition or passion.
scriptures: Job 39:7
He scorneth the multitude of the city, neither regardeth he the crying of the driver.
Exo 5:6
And Pharaoh commanded the same day the taskmasters of the people, and their officers, saying,
Exo 5:10
And the taskmasters of the people went out, and their officers, and they spake to the people, saying, Thus saith Pharaoh, I will not give you straw.
corruption_summary: Modern ambition-culture has taken the driver's whip and renamed it a virtue: to be driven is praised as admirable intensity, while Scripture's only extended picture of a driver is Pharaoh's taskmaster increasing a slave's burden.
corruption_paragraphs: "Driven" is offered today as the highest compliment a career can earn, borrowed without irony from Exodus 5, where the driver's whole function is to demand more work for less provision. The word has not lost its content; it has simply changed which side is expected to admire it.

Job 39:7 answers this from the other direction: the wild ass, made free by God, does not so much as hear the crying of the driver. Christ offers the believer the same freedom in substance — my yoke is easy — against every voluntary submission to a modern taskmaster's crying.
roots_summary: From nagas (Heb.), to press, drive, or exact, the word used of Pharaoh's taskmasters over the Israelites.
roots_lines: Driver in Job describes a cry the wild ass is free to ignore.
Driver in Exodus describes a demand no Israelite was free to ignore.
The taskmaster's power in Egypt is bondage administered by men over men.
Withholding straw while demanding the same quota is the driver's method, named plainly.
The exodus itself is the record of every driver's authority finally broken.
usage: The crying of the driver — a sound the free creature need not regard.
The taskmasters of the people... their officers — bondage with its full chain of command named.
I will not give you straw — the driver's method: more required, less provided.

pos: v. (past tense of eye; watched narrowly, often with suspicion or envy)
etymology: From eye, Anglo-Saxon eage — to watch or observe closely, especially with a fixed or hostile attention.
biblical_def:
Leah was tender eyed; but Rachel was beautiful and well favoured. And Saul eyed David from that day and forward.

Scripture's two uses of eyed sit at opposite ends of the same organ's meaning. Leah's description, tender eyed, is a plain physical note set beside Rachel's beauty, part of the ordinary honesty with which the narrative records both sisters without flattering either. Saul's eyed is a different thing entirely: from the day the women sang David's praises above his own, Saul eyed David, and the verb marks the exact hinge where royal favor curdled into murderous envy. Nothing physical changed in David; what changed was the fixed, watching, calculating attention Saul now trained on him. The same word that can note a plain feature of the face can also record the birth of an obsession, and Scripture leaves the reader to see which is which by what follows.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from EYE: to watch; to observe narrowly; to keep in view, often with a suspicious or envious attention.
webster_full: EYE, n. The organ of sight; also, look, aspect, or notice, as fixed on some object.
EYE, v.t. To fix the eye on; to look at; to observe narrowly.
To watch with jealousy or suspicion.
EYED, pp. Watched; observed with a fixed or narrow attention.
Applied in Scripture to Saul's suspicious, envious watching of David after his victories.
scriptures: Leah was tender eyed; but Rachel was beautiful and well favoured.
And Saul eyed David from that day and forward.
corruption_summary: A surveillance culture that constantly watches, tracks, and monitors others has learned to call this vigilance, ambition, or diligence, borrowing the language of care for what Scripture, in Saul's case, names plainly as envy.
corruption_paragraphs: Saul eyed David from the day the song of the women first praised David above him, and the text does not soften what follows: the eyeing is the seed of the spear thrown twice at David's head. Modern life, constantly watching others' success on a screen, calls this attentiveness rather than envy, but the fruit it produces is the same Saul's produced.
The remedy Scripture offers is not less watching in general but a different object for it — Hebrews commands looking unto Jesus, the same fixed attention Saul gave to David, now rightly aimed.
roots_summary: From ayin (Heb.), eye, the same root behind the evil eye of envy Christ names in Matthew 20:15.
roots_lines: Eyed can be a plain physical note, as of Leah's eyes.
Eyed can also mark the exact birth of envy, as of Saul's watching.
The women's song is the occasion; the eyeing is Saul's own response to it.
The spear thrown at David follows directly from the eyeing that preceded it.
Scripture elsewhere calls the envious watching eye an evil eye.
usage: Leah was tender eyed — an honest physical note, not a slight.
Saul eyed David from that day and forward — envy dated to a precise beginning.
The same verb that describes a face can describe the start of a murder.
